power.title: Power Analysis Check

table.text: Contrastingly, there was full support for Hypothesis 2 as the presence of watching eyes led to increased pro-environmental behaviour in the OSD task. This suggests that individuals responded to this cue of being observed to signal their environmental behavior (O' Keefe et al., 2026), thereby providing strong support for the validity of the OSD. Caution should be exercised however in interpreting this finding, because of the lower power of Study 2 due to the reduced sample size (see section 2.1). Despite the relatively large effect size observed here, a reliability power analysis suggests that it had only 70% power to detect such an effect. This coupled with the mixed overall findings for the watching eyes effect (Wang et al., 2024) suggests that further investigation of the possible role of social influence on the OSD is warranted. The existing findings are however promising, and further research that examines social influences on pro-environmental behaviours such as signalling in mating contexts (e.g., (Farmer & Farrelly, 2023; Farrelly & Bhogal, 2021; Palomo-Vélez et al., 2021) can make use of the OSD task in the future.

For study 1, a medium effect size (r = .3) (as with previous studies [Farrelly et al., 2024; Lange et al., 2018]), and 80% power with a corrected alpha level of .025 (due to controlling for multiple comparisons) required 102 participants. In total there were 104 (mean age = 21.3 years, SD = 4.6, 87% female) participants in Study 1. For study 2, the analysis to test Hypothesis 2 was used as this would require the larger sample. To detect a medium effect size with 80% power and an alpha level of .05 required a total sample size of 128 participants. Due to practical constraints of participant availability this was however not achieved and instead there were 96 (mean age = 21.4 years, SD = 6.2, 94% female) participants in Study 2. A total of 10 participants' data was removed across both studies due to not passing the inclusion criteria for the attention check questions (a minimum of two correct answers). stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Measures of actual pro-environmental behaviour are increasingly in environmental psychology due to their increased ecological validity over self-report measures.

Here we introduce a new such measure, the One-Shot Download Task (OSD), a brief online behavioural measure in which participants choose between incurring personal costs (completing a tedious task) or environmental costs (downloading unnecessary files associated with carbon emissions).

Two studies were conducted (Study 1: N = 104; Study 2: N = 96) that assessed the OSD's criterion validity by examining associations with measures of eco-anxiety, environmentally minded consumer behaviour and environmental attitudes, while Study 2 also tested whether social influence in the form of exposure to "watching eyes" stimuli increased pro-environmental choices in the task.

It was found that OSD scores positively correlated with environmentally minded consumer behaviour and the Preservation dimension of environmental attitudes, but not with eco-anxiety or Utilization attitudes.
Furthermore, participants exposed to watching eyes selected significantly more environmentally friendly options (higher scores on the OSD).

These findings provide initial evidence for the validity of the OSD as a measure of actual pro-environmental behaviour, demonstrating expected relationships with established environmental constructs and sensitivity to social influence.

Given its simplicity, low cost, and accessibility, the OSD offers a practical addition to the growing range of behavioural measures available to environmental psychological researchers, although further validation is warranted.
There has been an increased emphasis recently on the need to be able to accurately and objectively measure actual pro-environmental behavior (Lange, 2022; Lange et al., 2023).
text.formatted: There has been an increased emphasis recently on the need to be able to accurately and objectively measure actual pro-environmental behavior <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Lange, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Lange et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Such measures can offer more validity than self-report measures and can therefore be of greater predictive value.
This can benefit more applied investigations of pro-environmental behavior and/or successful real-world interventions.
As a result of this, several such measures have recently been introduced.

These include the Greater Goods Game (Klein et al., 2017), the Pro-Environmental Behavior task (Lange et al., 2018), the Tree task (Essl et al., 2025) the Work for Environmental Protection task (Lange & Dewitte, 2021), the Carbon Emissions task (S. Berger & Wyss, 2021) and the Behavioral Allocation task (Lange & Rieger, 2025).

text.text: All of these have been shown to be valid measures of pro-environmental behavior and subsequently used in further research.

However, as noted by Farrelly et al., (2024), these measures have practical limitations in terms of either requiring specialist equipment and/or requiring additional financial costs (such as payments to charities or participants [based on their decisions in the tasks] or for carbon offsetting).

text.text: In response, Farrelly et al., (2024) created the Email Conservation Task (ECT), an online measure of actual pro-environmental behavior that required participants to incur either the personal costs of taking time to complete a menial task or the environmental costs of receiving an unnecessary email which result in the release of CO 2 emissions.

text.text: As with other online measures of prosocial behaviour that rely on time (rather than finances) as the cost incurred (e.g., Farmer & Farrelly, 2023) it requires no further financial costs, making it a more accessible, cheap and inclusive measure of pro-environmental behavior for future research (Farrelly et al., 2024).

text.text: The current studies test a novel follow-up measure to the ECT which investigates individuals' proenvironmental behavior in a single choice rather than across a series of choices, as the ECT does.
Here we introduce the One-Shot Download Task (OSD), which is based on the potential environmental costs of another online activity, the downloading of large files (Farrelly, 2025).
text.formatted: Here we introduce the One-Shot Download Task (OSD), which is based on the potential environmental costs of another online activity, the downloading of large files <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Farrelly, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In this task, participants will, as with the ECT, be required to choose to either incur the personal costs of time spent on a menial task (a number discrimination task as is used in the ECT) or the environmental costs of downloading unnecessary files.

Unlike the ECT, the OSD features a single choice an individual needs to make with varying levels of personal costs (number of trials of the number discriminations) and environmental costs (size of file to download).
Individuals therefore who choose options with greater personal cost and lesser environmental costs in the OSD will display higher levels of pro-environmental behavior.

As a result, it is hoped that the OSD will also be beneficial in terms of accessibility and inclusivity that the ECT provides but will also now offer a quicker and more immediate measure of pro-environmental behavior, in a single question.
In order to test the validity of the OSD, two separate studies were conducted.

Firstly, to assess its criterion validity Study 1 explored how scores on the OSD related to other existing self-report measures of environmentalism, that of eco-anxiety (Hogg et al., 2021) and environmental consumer behavior (Sudbury-Riley & Kohlbacher, 2016), whereas Study 2 explored environmental attitudes (Milfont & Duckitt, 2010).

text.text: Furthermore, Study 2 explored how social influence may affect people's behavior on the OSD.

Previous research has shown how this can increase pro-environmental behavior (Berger, 2019; Farrelly & Bhogal, 2021; Griskevicius et al., 2010), highlighting how the visibility of such behaviors allow individuals to signal their environmentalism (O' Keefe et al., 2026).

text.text: Power analyses were conducted using JAMOVI to determine the required sample size for each study.

For study 1, a medium effect size (r = .3) (as with previous studies [Farrelly et al., 2024; Lange et al., 2018]), and 80% power with a corrected alpha level of .025 (due to controlling for multiple comparisons) required 102 participants.

text.text: In total there were 104 (mean age = 21.3 years, SD = 4.6, 87% female) participants in Study 1.
For study 2, the analysis to test Hypothesis 2 was used as this would require the larger sample.
To detect a medium effect size with 80% power and an alpha level of .05 required a total sample size of 128 participants.
Due to practical constraints of participant availability this was however not achieved and instead there were 96 (mean age = 21.4 years, SD = 6.2, 94% female) participants in Study 2.
A total of 10 participants' data was removed across both studies due to not passing the inclusion criteria for the attention check questions (a minimum of two correct answers).
All participants were undergraduate psychology students who completed the study in return for course credits.
This study was approved by the authors' university's institutional ethics committee.
Environmental attitudes are measured across twelve subscales, with two questions in the EAI-24 for each subscale.
These combine to measure to higher order factors, Preservation (i.e., preserving nature and other species from human interference) and Utilization (i.e., using nature for human objectives).
Participants' scores for these two were used, and Cronbach's alpha of .74 for Preservation and .73 for Utilization were found in the present study.

This 13 item self-report measure assesses the frequency of thoughts of climate related worry over the past two weeks using a 4-point Likert scale, with higher overall scores indicating greater levels of eco-anxiety.
A Cronbach's alpha score of .9 was found for HEAS in this study.
This 10 item self-report questionnaire assesses sustainable purchasing behaviours (e.g., buying ecofriendly products).
Responses were provided on a 5-point Likert scale, with higher scores indicating greater engagement in sustainable consumerism.
A Cronbach's alpha score of .89 was found for EMCB in this study.
The London Face Database (DeBruine & Jones, 2017) was used to source images, and three male and three female images were randomly selected to be used.

>Results
text.formatted: <head n="3." >Results</head>

text.text: Pearson's correlations were conducted and sequential Bonferroni adjustments used to calculate an initial alpha level of 0.025 by dividing the standard alpha level (0.05) by the number of tests (2) in each study to control for multiple comparisons.

It was found that scores on the OSC task significantly correlated with scores on the EMCB (r = .28, p = .004, 95% CI [0.45, 0.09]) and the Preservation factor of the EAI-24 (r = .28, p = .006, 95% CI [0.45, 0.08]), but not with either the HEAS (r = .01, p = .95, 95% CI [0.2, 0-.19]) or the Utilization factor of the EAI-24 (r = .11, p = .3, 95% CI [0.30, -0.09]).
An independent-samples t-test was conducted to compare participants' OSD task scores when in the presence of eyes or without.
It was found that participants in the presence of a pair of eyes scored significantly higher on the task than those who were not (t = 2.51, p = .01, d = .53), see figure 2
text.formatted: It was found that participants in the presence of a pair of eyes scored significantly higher on the task than those who were not (t = 2.51, p = .01, d = .53), see figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">2</ref>

text.text: Firstly, there was partial support for Hypothesis 1, as it was found that participants' scores on the OSD were significantly and positively correlated with their EMCB score and also the preservation factor of their EAI-24 score.
This is consistent with the links between self-report measures and other pro-environmental behavior tasks, as are the size of these relationships that were found (Delcourt et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This is consistent with the links between self-report measures and other pro-environmental behavior tasks, as are the size of these relationships that were found <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Delcourt et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: No such relationship however was found with the HEAS, which is perhaps not surprising, as a recent meta-analysis found a great variation in possible links between eco-anxiety and pro-environmental behavior (Davì et al., 2026) and was particularly weak for individual behavior (such as was the case with the OSD).

text.text: Furthermore the lack of a positive correlation between the OSD and the Utilization factor of the EAI-24 was also perhaps to be expected, as the latter's more anthropocentric focus has previously been found to not relate to environmental behaviors (Milfont & Duckitt, 2006).

text.text: Overall these findings provide further support for the multidimensionality of pro-environmental behavior (Lange, 2024).

text.text: Contrastingly, there was full support for Hypothesis 2 as the presence of watching eyes led to increased pro-environmental behaviour in the OSD task.
This suggests that individuals responded to this cue of being observed to signal their environmental behavior (O' Keefe et al., 2026), thereby providing strong support for the validity of the OSD.

text.text: Caution should be exercised however in interpreting this finding, because of the lower power of Study 2 due to the reduced sample size (see section 2.1).
Despite the relatively large effect size observed here, a reliability power analysis suggests that it had only 70% power to detect such an effect.
This coupled with the mixed overall findings for the watching eyes effect (Wang et al., 2024) suggests that further investigation of the possible role of social influence on the OSD is warranted.

text.text: The existing findings are however promising, and further research that examines social influences on pro-environmental behaviours such as signalling in mating contexts (e.g., (Farmer & Farrelly, 2023; Farrelly & Bhogal, 2021; Palomo-Vélez et al., 2021) can make use of the OSD task in the future.
text.formatted: The existing findings are however promising, and further research that examines social influences on pro-environmental behaviours such as signalling in mating contexts (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Farmer & Farrelly, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Farrelly & Bhogal, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Palomo-Vélez et al., 2021)</ref> can make use of the OSD task in the future.

text.text: As well as reduced power in Study 2, other limitations include the relatively low environmental costs of the OSD (file downloads) as was similarly the case with unnecessary emails in the ECT.

Also, similarly to the ECT, the OSD is however intended to act as an experimental means to measure pro-environmental behavior and as such utilises environmental costs that are of similar size to those of other similar measures (Lange et al., 2018; Farrelly et al., 2024).

text.text: Future research can therefore investigate how varying the personal and environmental costs in the OSD task alters individuals' choices.

Overall the findings presented here suggest the OSD task can make a valuable contribution to the existing canon of experimental measures of actual pro-environmental behavior and further address the necessity for more diversity and ability we have to measure pro-environmentalism (Lange et al., 2023; Nielsen et al., 2024).

text.text: Due to its low financial costs and simplicity of its single item measure, the OSD can act as a valuable experimental method that is more accessible to a wider range of environmental psychology researchers than other existing measures.

As a potential starting point for new research paradigms, the OSD can provide the preliminary answers as to how we can alter people's behavior when it comes to climate change, laying the foundations for further real-world applications and interventions.
